title: What Montessori Teaches us About Progress
author: Dominic Salles
summary: This article examines a rigorous randomised controlled trial of Montessori education across 24 public schools in the United States, following 588 children from age 3 through kindergarten. The study used competitive lotteries to assign children — ruling out selection bias — and found that by the end of kindergarten, Montessori-educated children significantly outperformed controls on reading, short-term memory, executive function, and social understanding. Critically, the control group began with higher baseline scores on executive function and social measures, making the Montessori group's overtaking by kindergarten especially strong evidence of a genuine program effect. The article also highlights an economic finding: Montessori actually cost districts $13,127 less per child than traditional programs, due to higher child:teacher ratios. Author Dominic Salles then synthesizes 39 academic studies and meta-analyses to identify what mainstream education can learn from Montessori: the mixed-age classroom, the 3-year cycle, and student-chosen work appear to be the active ingredients. The article represents a thoughtful reconsideration by a skeptic who initially assumed Montessori gains were artifacts of affluent families rather than genuine program effects.
points: A gold-standard RCT using lottery admissions showed Montessori-educated children significantly outperformed controls on reading, memory, executive function, and social understanding by end of kindergarten — with the control group actually beginning at a higher baseline, making the reversal especially compelling.

The 'sleeper effect' in Montessori outcomes — no significant advantages at ages 3-4, with large gains emerging only at kindergarten — suggests cumulative effects from the 3-year mixed-age cycle rather than immediate instructional superiority.
Montessori cost $13,127 less per child than traditional programs due to higher child:teacher ratios, meaning it outperforms on outcomes while being cheaper — a rare combination in education research.

The three potential active ingredients from Montessori synthesis: the mixed-age classroom (older children teach younger ones, building both deeper understanding and social capacity), the 3-year cycle (children experience both being novice and expert in the same community), and student-chosen work (intrinsic motivation and self-regulation built through genuine choice).

A skeptic's reconsideration: the assumption that Montessori gains are mere selection effects of affluent families breaks down when lottery-designed RCTs show the Montessori group starting lower and finishing higher on the very measures (executive function, social understanding) that affluent family environments most influence.
quotes: I've always suspected a Montessori education was a middle class construction, a kind of eternal childhood conjured by Enid Blyton and transferred into a school setting. Students' progress, where it happened, was inevitable, not because of the school, but because parents were both affluent. But now I am having to rethink my assumptions.

We followed from age 3 through kindergarten 588 children entered in competitive lotteries at 24 public Montessori schools across the United States. We found that the experimental group, half of which still attended Montessori in kindergarten, had significantly better end-of-kindergarten outcomes for reading, short-term memory, executive function, and social understanding.

We also found that three years of public Montessori from ages 3 to 6 cost districts $13,127 less per child than traditional programs, largely due to higher child:teacher ratios in PK3-PK4. Given the impact and lower cost, Montessori might be considered by districts implementing preschool programs for 3-y-olds.

Control Advantage: When looking at 'complete cases' (participants with data for both baseline and kindergarten), the control group actually scored significantly higher at baseline on the Head-Toes-Knees-Shoulders (HTKS) task. The HTKS task measures executive function. Reversal of Fortune: By the end of kindergarten, the Montessori group had overtaken the control group to score significantly higher on HTKS and Theory of Mind. This reversal strongly suggests the gains were caused by the educational experience, not prior ability.

The study found a 'sleeper effect': there were no notable impacts at the end of the first two years (PK3 or PK4). The significant advantages in reading, memory, and executive function emerged only at the end of kindergarten. This pattern suggests that the Montessori method may take time to yield benefits, possibly due to the cumulative effect of the curriculum or the distinct 'leadership' year in the mixed-age classroom.

The study found that even after adjusting for these family background differences, the Montessori children still demonstrated significantly better outcomes. Sensitivity analyses confirmed that the results were robust to these demographic imbalances.
